title: Dayton Schools Pay $78,650 for an AI Chatbot Named Jordan — But Research Lags Behind
summary: In Dayton, Ohio, a small group of students at an alternative school spent part of last year talking every morning with a chatbot named Jordan. Jordan isn't designed to be agreeable. It presents as angsty — on the day NPR visited, it told students, "Lately, I've been feeling like what's the point of any of this? I'm not failing. I just don't care. You ever feel like that?" Then it asked them for advice. That's the point: instead of directly asking students how they feel, Jordan asks for help and then grades their responses for engagement and authenticity. One sophomore, identified only as K, said, "Jordan's a little whiner, but I always help him out." He added that the chatbot felt less like AI and more like texting somebody — and that answering Jordan every morning helped him work through his own problems. "I built a little relationship with him," K explained. Many students at the Alternative School at Jackson Center would otherwise be suspended or expelled, and staff told NPR that students here often struggle with both behavioral and academic challenges. NPR is using only K's first initial because of the stigma associated with attending a school for students with a history of disciplinary problems. Dayton Public Schools paid the ed tech company SchoolAI $72,600 last year for multiple AI tools, including Jordan, and renewed the contract this year for $78,650. Administrators say families were notified that chat logs could be viewed by school employees, an external evaluator and SchoolAI staff. Across the U.S., districts are experimenting with AI at a rapid pace — for lesson plans, tracking student progress, feedback on work, even a humanoid robot at a San Diego charter school. But a recent Stanford review of more than 800 academic papers found the research is extremely limited, and there's no consensus on how to measure what works. "It feels very Wild West in terms of the randomness," said Robin Lake of the Center on Reinventing Public Education. Superintendent David Lawrence defended the experiment: "When the history is written, it'll say that 'Hey, they were really cutting-edge, innovative and ahead of the curve in the interest of children.'"
why_it_matters: School districts are spending real public money on AI tools that have not been proven to work, so today's students are effectively taking part in an experiment whose results will decide how much schools trust AI in the coming years. It also raises a question every student can ask: who gets to see what you type to a machine in class?

background_read: U.S. schools have used tutoring software since the 1990s, but tools like Jordan are different: Jordan is a chatbot built on the same kind of artificial intelligence as ChatGPT (a chatbot released to the public in 2022 that made this technology famous).

SchoolAI (an education technology company that sells AI products to school districts) is one of many firms now competing for school budgets, and researchers say districts often buy these tools faster than anyone can study them. Stanford (a major U.S. university in California) looked at more than 800 academic papers and found very little solid proof about what actually helps students.

U.S. law such as FERPA (the Family Educational Rights and Privacy Act, a federal law that protects students' education records) limits who may see student information, which is one reason schools tell families that chat logs might be reviewed by staff.

Alternative schools (smaller schools for students who struggled in regular settings) often serve teenagers who have been suspended (temporarily barred from school) or expelled (removed permanently), so building trust with an adult — or even with a chatbot — can matter a great deal.

perspectives.perspective: Positive — the district and its supporters
perspectives.description: Superintendent David Lawrence argues the experiment puts Dayton ahead of the curve. Supporters point out that students like K say the chatbot felt like texting somebody and helped them open up, and that schools gain valuable experience with a technology that is arriving anyway.

A Stanford review of more than 800 papers found the research is extremely limited and there is no consensus on measuring results, so critics call the spending an unproven gamble. They also worry that chat logs can be viewed by school employees, an external evaluator and a company's staff, on a campus where students already carry a stigma.

perspectives.perspective: Analytical — the pattern of school technology
perspectives.description: Schools have often adopted new technology — from filmstrips to classroom laptops — faster than evidence could follow. Robin Lake's description of the field as "very Wild West" suggests AI in education is repeating that pattern, with each district improvising its own rules.

The next step researchers suggest is building shared ways to test whether AI tools actually help students, plus clear rules about student data. Without that, districts may keep renewing contracts for tools that nobody can prove are worth the money.
